questions.question: In which stage is leadership shared among the founder's children?
questions.explanation: In a sibling partnership (second generation) ownership and management are shared among brothers and sisters, so leadership moves from one decision-maker to a group of peers.

questions.question: A third or later generation business owned and managed by cousins is called a...
questions.explanation: A cousin consortium has fragmented ownership and needs formal corporate governance to avoid deadlock.

questions.question: Why does conflict arise when family principles are applied to business decisions?
options: The family system rewards unconditional loyalty, while the business needs accountability for performance
The family system is always wrong
Business rules never apply to relatives
Families have no interest in profit
questions.explanation: The family system is organised around nurturing and loyalty whatever a member contributes. The business system runs on efficiency, profitability and merit, so applying one to the other creates friction.

questions.question: Which three sub-systems make up the Three-Circle Model?
questions.explanation: Tagiuri and Davis described a family firm as three overlapping sub-systems: family, ownership and management.

questions.question: How many stakeholder sectors does the Three-Circle Model produce?
questions.explanation: The overlap of the three circles creates seven sectors, each with its own priorities and potential conflicts.

questions.question: In the lecturer's numbering, which sector holds family members who own shares, sit on the board and work as managers?
questions.explanation: Sector 7, family owner-employees, is the nexus of control. Sources number the sectors differently, so name the group as well as the number.

questions.question: A family member works in the business but holds no shares. Which sector is this, in the lecturer's numbering?
questions.explanation: Family employees work in the business without equity. Family owners (sector 5) hold shares without working day to day.

questions.question: What is socio-emotional wealth?
options: The money a family earns from dividends
The non-financial value and emotional returns family members get from the firm
The total salary paid to relatives
The value of the firm's property
questions.explanation: Socio-emotional wealth is the non-financial value and emotional returns family members get from owning and running the firm.

questions.question: In the FIBER model, what does the B stand for?
questions.explanation: FIBER: family control and influence, identification of the family, binding social ties, emotional attachment, and renewal of family bonds.

questions.question: A successor stays in the firm mainly from fear of financial loss. Which commitment type is this?
questions.explanation: Cost-based commitment ('have to') comes from fear of financial loss and leads to passive compliance. Need-based commitment comes from desperation or having no outside job.

questions.question: Which commitment type gives the best performance and proactive innovation?
questions.explanation: Desire-based commitment comes from real passion for the business and its goals.

questions.question: What are co-preneurs?
options: A parent and child in the same firm
A married couple who jointly own and manage a business
Two siblings who inherit a firm
questions.explanation: Co-preneurs are husband-and-wife teams. They share trust and a financial vision, but disputes can spill into home life.

questions.question: According to the notes, how long should prospective successors work outside the family firm first?
questions.explanation: Working outside for two to five years builds objective skills, confidence and credibility.

questions.question: In the predator/parasite conflict, who sees the active managers as predators?
questions.explanation: Non-working shareholders see active managers as predators who take profit through salaries, bonuses and perks. The managers see them as parasites who want dividends without working.

questions.question: What is the recommended way to handle in-laws who join the business?
options: Assign them to separate branches or roles that do not overlap
Give them the most senior roles
Keep them out of the family council only
Pay them more than other staff
questions.explanation: Separate branches or non-overlapping roles reduce jealousy and claims of favouritism.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of Lansky's five guidelines for a family retreat?
options: Exclude younger members until they hold shares
questions.explanation: The guidelines are clear purpose, attainable goals, structured agenda, inclusive participation (every member may speak) and consensus rather than mere agreement.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the six core components of a family constitution?
questions.explanation: The six components are core values, decision-making protocols, family benefits, next-generation onboarding, dispute resolution and philanthropic ambitions.

questions.question: What is a family council?
options: A tax body for family firms
A meeting held once at a retreat
A formal body of family representatives that meets periodically to coordinate family-business policy
questions.explanation: A family council coordinates family-business policy, represents the family to the board and, according to the notes, drafts and enforces the constitution.

questions.question: Which is NOT an alternative succession pathway when family succession is not viable?
options: Automatic transfer to the eldest child
questions.explanation: The alternatives are a professional non-family general manager, interim management until heirs are ready, and an outright sale. Transfer should depend on competence, not birth order.

questions.question: Why should tax minimisation not decide how ownership is transferred?
options: Tax does not matter in family firms
Operating effectiveness must come first; tax savings should not create an unworkable ownership structure
Tax rules only apply to non-family owners
questions.explanation: Minimising tax matters, but the ownership structure has to work for the business.

questions.question: Which is a responsibility of the senior generation in succession planning?
options: Designing life plans around the firm
Preparing a personal action plan to gain skills
questions.explanation: The senior generation communicates about retirement, plans in writing, enforces accountability, develops owners and designs an exit. The other options are junior-generation responsibilities.

questions.question: In the Iaccarino & Son case, what had Fran failed to do when he joined the firm?
questions.explanation: Fran joined without an ownership position and later found that his father would not let go of power.

questions.question: Which statement best matches what the Iaccarino & Son case says about the recession?
options: It reached the firm late, in 2010 and 2011, and the firm could not shrink fast enough to absorb the shock
The firm felt it at once and recovered quickly
The firm was unaffected and closed for other reasons
Sales fell in 2008 and never recovered
questions.explanation: The firm was a lagging indicator of the downturn. It lost three projects in a day, cut margins to win work and filed for bankruptcy in 2012, a year after its highest sales.
